pos: n. (proper name; king of Sodom in the days of Abram)
etymology: Hebrew Bera', of uncertain meaning; readings as gift or as in evil have both been proposed, neither with certainty.
biblical_def: Bera is named once: “That these made war with Bera king of Sodom, and with Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, and Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar” (Genesis 14:2). He is the king of Sodom in the war of the four kings against the five — defeated by Chedorlaomer, his city plundered, his people and Abram's nephew Lot carried off, and then rescued by Abram with three hundred and eighteen trained servants. What happens afterward is the point of the chapter. Two kings came out to meet the returning Abram. Melchizedek king of Salem brought bread and wine and blessed him, and Abram gave him tithes of all. The king of Sodom offered a bargain: give me the persons and take the goods. Abram refused him with an oath, so that no man could say he had made Abram rich. The contrast is deliberate and total: a priest-king who gives and blesses, and a city-king who trades. “I have lift up mine hand unto the LORD, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth” (Genesis 14:22) is how Abram declined the offer, and Hebrews 7 builds a whole doctrine of Christ's priesthood out of the other king in the scene.

scriptures: That these made war with Bera king of Sodom, and with Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, and Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar.
And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.
And Abram said to the king of Sodom, I have lift up mine hand unto the LORD, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth,
For this Melchisedec, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him;
corruption_summary: Genesis 14 is read as a fragment of ancient war annals; the chapter is built to set a priest-king beside a merchant-king.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 14 is often treated as an archaic insertion with no theological purpose, a scrap of campaign record. Its structure says otherwise. The battle occupies sixteen verses; the meeting afterward occupies the rest, and it sets two kings side by side — Melchizedek who brings bread and wine and blesses, Bera who proposes a division of spoil. Abram tithes to the one and refuses the other.

The principle to recover is that the chapter is Christological by design, not by later allegory. Hebrews 7 reasons from Melchizedek's priesthood — without recorded genealogy, king and priest at once, greater than Abraham who paid him tithes — to the priesthood of Christ after that order. The king of Sodom is in the text so that the reader will see what Abram would not take and from whom he would receive.

pos: n. (proper name; king of Gomorrah in the days of Abram)
etymology: Hebrew Birsha', commonly read with wickedness, from a preposition with resha', wickedness — though the derivation is not certain.
biblical_def: Birsha is named once, beside Bera: “That these made war with Bera king of Sodom, and with Birsha king of Gomorrah” (Genesis 14:2). He is king of the city that would become, with Sodom, Scripture's permanent byword for judgment. At the time of this war the cities were prosperous and the plain was well watered, “even as the garden of the LORD” (Genesis 13:10), which is why Lot had chosen it. The destruction was still years off. That gap is the thing worth marking. Birsha reigned, lost a war, was rescued by Abram, and went home to a city under a sentence not yet executed; and the men of Sodom and Gomorrah went on as they had. “They did eat, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded; but the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all” (Luke 17:28-29) — which is how Christ Himself used the history, as a warning about the ordinariness of life on the day judgment falls. The dictionary holds the destruction of these cities as an event, because our Lord did.

corruption_summary: Sodom and Gomorrah are reduced to legend; Christ and the apostles treat the overthrow as history and as warning.
corruption_paragraphs: The destruction of the cities of the plain is widely handled as folklore attached to a geological feature. The dictionary holds it as an event, on the authority of the Lord Jesus, who dated it to the day Lot went out and used it to describe the suddenness of His own return, and of Peter, who calls the overthrow an ensample to those that after should live ungodly.

The principle to recover is that judgment falls on a day that looks like the others. They ate, drank, bought, sold, planted and builded, and the fire came that same day. Birsha king of Gomorrah lived a whole reign under a sentence, and the plain was like the garden of the LORD while he did. Delay is not acquittal and prosperity is not safety.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the wise men whom Solomon's wisdom excelled)
etymology: Hebrew Kalkol, commonly read sustenance or he sustains, from a root meaning to nourish or maintain. 1 Chronicles 2:6 names a Calcol among the sons of Zerah of Judah.
biblical_def: Chalcol is named once, and in a comparison: “For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol: and his fame was in all nations round about” (1 Kings 4:31). The writer is establishing the greatness of Solomon's wisdom, and to do it he names the four men his readers would have reckoned the wisest in the world. Chalcol is one of the four. That is a strange sort of fame — to be remembered in Scripture as the standard somebody else surpassed. And the context makes the source of the surpassing plain: “And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart” (1 Kings 4:29). Solomon's wisdom was a gift, asked for and granted, not an achievement he could set against Chalcol's. The dictionary adds the end of the story, since Scripture does: the wisest man alive was turned aside by his wives in his old age, and the wisdom was not enough to keep him. “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3) is said of Another, who was never turned.

corruption_summary: Wisdom is treated as a possession that secures its holder; Solomon's was a gift, and it did not keep him.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account of wisdom makes it an acquired capacity that renders a man proof against folly. 1 Kings tells a different story in the space of seven chapters: God gave Solomon wisdom exceeding much, his fame went out to all nations, and when he was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not perfect with the LORD.

The principle to recover is that wisdom is a gift to be asked for and kept by grace, not a fortification. The Preacher who wrote that all was vanity had the largest mind of his age and finished it saying so. The treasures of wisdom are hid in Christ (Colossians 2:3), and only there are they safe from the man who holds them.

pos: n. (proper name; a place trading with Tyre in Ezekiel's lament)
etymology: Hebrew Kilmad, of uncertain reference; proposals have placed it in Assyria or Media, and some read the word as part of a phrase rather than a place-name.
biblical_def: Chilmad is named once: “Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad, were thy merchants” (Ezekiel 27:23). The verse belongs to the great lament over Tyre, a chapter that catalogues the commerce of the ancient world in extraordinary detail — silver from Tarshish, horses from Togarmah, ivory and ebony, emeralds and fine linen, wheat and honey and oil and balm, iron and spices, lambs and rams and goats, with named cities supplying each. Then the chapter turns: “The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more” (Ezekiel 27:36). The dictionary notes why the inventory is so long. Ezekiel lists the whole of Tyre's glory in order to show the scale of what God was about to take down, and the reason is given in the next chapter: the prince of Tyre said, I am a god, I sit in the seat of God. Pride at the summit of trade. Chilmad is one name in the ledger of a city whose wealth was real and whose fall was certain.

corruption_summary: Commercial greatness is read as its own justification; Ezekiel inventories Tyre's wealth to measure the fall of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 27 is sometimes mined as an economic source and admired as a portrait of ancient trade, with the lament's purpose set aside. The chapter is not an appreciation. It is a dirge, and the detail exists to establish the height from which the city was to come down; the following chapter gives the charge, that the prince of Tyre had said in his heart, I am a God.

The principle to recover is that prosperity does not confer immunity and pride at the top of it invites the fall. “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). Chilmad's merchants did real business with a real city, and the ledger survives in Scripture as the measure of a judgment.

pos: n. (proper name; a place in the wilderness named in the opening of Deuteronomy)
etymology: Hebrew Di-zahab, place of gold, from a relative element with zahab, gold. The name suggests a locality where gold was found or worked.
biblical_def: Dizahab is named once, and the verse it closes is the title of a book: “These be the words which Moses spake unto all Israel on this side Jordan in the wilderness, in the plain over against the Red sea, between Paran, and Tophel, and Laban, and Hazeroth, and Dizahab” (Deuteronomy 1:1). Moses is about to deliver the sermons that make up Deuteronomy, and the first thing the book does is fix the place and the time — a named plain among named landmarks, and then the date: “in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month” (Deuteronomy 1:3). Between those two verses stands the saddest parenthesis in the Pentateuch: “There are eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of mount Seir unto Kadeshbarnea” (Deuteronomy 1:2). Eleven days' walk; forty years taken. The dictionary marks what the arrangement is doing. Moses locates his final sermons at the end of a detour that unbelief had made out of a fortnight's march, and the name place of gold stands in the list of landmarks they had wandered among. The cost of not believing God is counted in that parenthesis.

corruption_summary: Deuteronomy is assigned to a much later century; the book opens by fixing its own place, day and month.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy is the standard case for late composition, commonly assigned to the seventh century and attached to Josiah's reform. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship, and notes that the book's first three verses are a claim no later composer needed to make: a named plain between five named landmarks, on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year, spoken by Moses to all Israel.

The principle to recover is the one the parenthesis teaches. Eleven days' journey became forty years, and Hebrews gives the reason without softening it: “So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19). Unbelief is not a neutral hesitation; it is the thing that turns a fortnight into a generation and leaves a people wandering among places with names like place of gold.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Paltiel, prince of Issachar)
etymology: Hebrew 'Azzan, very strong or sharp, from the root 'azaz, to be strong — the same root behind Azaz, Uzziah and Aziza.
biblical_def: Azzan is named once, and only as a father: “And the prince of the tribe of the children of Issachar, Paltiel the son of Azzan” (Numbers 34:26). His son was one of the twelve tribal princes appointed to divide the land of Canaan. The commission is set out at the head of the list: “These are the names of the men which shall divide the land unto you: Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun” (Numbers 34:17), and then one prince named from each tribe, and the closing verse: “These are they whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance unto the children of Israel in the land of Canaan” (Numbers 34:29). The dictionary marks the care of the arrangement. The division of the promised land was not left to whoever had the strongest claim or the loudest voice; the LORD named a priest, a captain, and one man from every tribe, so that no tribe could say it had been apportioned by its rivals. God is not careless with an inheritance He has sworn, and He is not careless about the fairness of its distribution either.

corruption_paragraphs: The division of the land is commonly described as the stronger tribes taking what they could hold, with the allotment lists written afterward to legitimise it. Numbers 34 was written before the division and names the commissioners in advance: a priest, a captain, and one prince from each of the twelve tribes, with the lot to settle the portions.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is exact about justice among His own people. He had sworn the land; He also appointed the procedure by which it would be shared, so that the apportioning could not be captured by the strong. A father named very strong appears in Scripture because his son was put on that commission.

pos: n. (proper name; a deliverer named by Samuel, and a Manassite)
etymology: Hebrew Bedan, of uncertain meaning; a reading in judgment or son of judgment has been proposed. Some take the name in 1 Samuel 12:11 as a variant for Barak.
biblical_def: Bedan is named twice, of two men. The first stands in Samuel's farewell address: “And the LORD sent Jerubbaal, and Bedan, and Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side, and ye dwelled safe” (1 Samuel 12:11). The second is a Manassite: “And the sons of Ulam; Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 7:17). The first is the interesting one, because he is named among the judges and does not appear in the book of Judges under that name; some therefore read him as Barak, others as a judge otherwise unrecorded. The dictionary leaves the question open rather than deciding it for tidiness. What matters is the argument Samuel is making. He recites the deliverers — Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, Samuel — and the subject of every clause is the LORD sent. Israel had just demanded a king because Nahash was coming, forgetting that every past rescue had come without one. “Only fear the LORD, and serve him in truth with all your heart: for consider how great things he hath done for you” (1 Samuel 12:24).

corruption_paragraphs: Because Bedan does not appear in the book of Judges, the verse is often emended or offered as evidence of a confused text. The dictionary records the uncertainty honestly and declines both the emendation and the conclusion. Judges does not claim to name every deliverer, and Samuel is reciting history his hearers knew, not citing a book.

The principle to recover is the one Samuel is pressing. Four deliverers are named and the subject throughout is the LORD sent; Israel's demand for a king was a confession that she had stopped believing it. “When the LORD your God was your king” (1 Samuel 12:12) is the rebuke, and the remedy is in verse 24: fear the LORD and consider how great things He hath done for you.

pos: n. (proper name; prince of the Reubenites, carried captive by Assyria)
etymology: Hebrew Be'erah, a well, from be'er — the same root as in Beeri and Beersheba.
biblical_def: Beerah is named once, and the verse is a sentence of exile: “Beerah his son, whom Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria carried away captive: he was prince of the Reubenites” (1 Chronicles 5:6). He held the highest office in his tribe and the Chronicler records him only to say where he ended. Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh were the first of Israel to go into captivity, taken from their pastureland east of Jordan, and the Chronicler gives the reason in the same chapter without flinching: they “transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land” (1 Chronicles 5:25), and God stirred up the Assyrian kings against them. The dictionary notes that the office did not shelter the man. A prince of Reuben went into Assyria with his people, because leaders are not exempted from the judgments their people incur and are generally held to a stricter account. “For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God” (1 Peter 4:17). Beerah's name means a well, and he was carried away from his water to a river called Gozan.

corruption_summary: Office is assumed to shelter its holder; a prince of Reuben went into Assyria with the tribe he led.
corruption_paragraphs: Position is widely treated as insulation, and religious position most of all. The Chronicler names Beerah as prince of the Reubenites in the same clause in which he records his deportation. The office is stated and the captivity is stated, and the one plainly did not prevent the other.

The principle to recover is that leaders are judged with, and more strictly than, those they lead. “For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God” (1 Peter 4:17), and James warns teachers that they shall receive the greater condemnation. A prince carried away to the river Gozan is the Old Testament form of the same warning.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Zophah of the tribe of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Be'era, a well, from be'er — the same element as in Beerah the Reubenite, though the men and the tribes differ.
biblical_def: Beera is named once, last in a list: “Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera” (1 Chronicles 7:37). He belongs to the tribe of Asher, and the dictionary keeps him distinct from Beerah the Reubenite prince of 1 Chronicles 5:6 — the names are near, the men are not the same. The Asher genealogy closes with a verdict worth setting beside the exile of Reuben a chapter and a half earlier: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Asher had been blessed by Jacob with oil and dainties and by Moses with his foot dipped in oil, and the tribe is never recorded as producing a judge or a king. It appears at the edges of the history and is well spoken of. The New Testament gives it one more line: Anna the prophetess, who waited in the temple and saw the infant Christ, was of the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36). A tribe with no great men had a woman who recognised the Lord when she saw Him.

corruption_summary: A tribe without famous men is counted negligible; Asher is commended in the record and supplied a witness at the temple.
corruption_paragraphs: Significance is measured by prominent names, and on that measure Asher is the least interesting tribe in Israel: no judge, no king, no prophet in the Old Testament. The Chronicler nonetheless calls its heads choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes, and Moses had blessed it with oil and the goodwill of its brethren.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faithfulness is not fame. Asher's one New Testament mention is Anna, an old widow who had not left the temple and who knew the Christ in a forty-day-old infant. A tribe that produced no rulers produced her, and Luke thought her worth a paragraph.

pos: n. (proper name; a chief of the people who sealed Nehemiah's covenant)
etymology: Hebrew 'Azzur, commonly read helper or he who helps, from the root 'azar, to help — the root behind Azariah, Eliezer and Ezra.
biblical_def: Azzur is named once, and his verse is three words: “Ater, Hizkijah, Azzur” (Nehemiah 10:17). He is one of the chiefs of the people whose seals closed the covenant of Nehemiah 10, the document that begins “Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah” (Nehemiah 10:1) and runs on through eighty-odd names before reaching the obligations themselves. His name means helper, and that is the whole of what the record does with him: he helped, by setting his seal where it counted. The dictionary ends this night's work on a name like this deliberately. Nothing is known of Azzur but that he signed a promise to walk in God's law, to keep the sabbath, to bring the firstfruits and the tithes, and not to forsake the house of his God. That is not a small thing to be remembered for; it is nearly the only thing worth being remembered for. “And we will not forsake the house of our God” (Nehemiah 10:39) is the last clause of the document he sealed, and his name is on it.

corruption_summary: A life is counted significant by its visible achievements; Scripture remembers a man for a seal on a promise he kept.
corruption_paragraphs: The measure of a life in common use is accomplishment that others can see and name, and by that measure a man known only for a signature has done nothing. Nehemiah 10 disagrees in the plainest way available to a book: it gives eighty-odd names, Azzur's among them, and then the obligations those names undertook, and preserves the whole for two and a half thousand years.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that covenant faithfulness is the substance of a life well spent. “And we will not forsake the house of our God” (Nehemiah 10:39) is what Azzur put his seal to, and the Scripture that keeps his name keeps it for that reason and no other. It is enough.
